newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Teachers join Serbia's anti-government protests.
newsitem.headline: Teachers join Serbia's anti-government protests.

text.p: The Serbian opposition prepared on Thursday for more demonstrations, ignoring warnings by a ruling Socialist hardliner to get off the streets now that their local election victories have been restored.

Some 7,000 teachers demonstrated in front of the Serbian parliament on Thursday demanding higher wages and improvement of school conditions, adding to the wave of protests that has rocked Serbia for the past 86 days.

Wary of President Slobodan Milosevic's subterfuge, the three leaders of the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition have said their protests will continue until the very last opposition councillor takes office -- which is expected to happen next week.

But Zajedno and their student allies, who fought the November election fraud by mounting daily demonstrations for 12 weeks, vowed not to let up the pressure for additional reforms either on the streets or through a dialogue.
Civil disobedience was one of the forms of pressure suggested and the Zajedno mayor of Kragujevac called on his citizens on Thursday to do just that.

"I invite the citizens of Kragujevac to citizens' disobedience. I call on them not to pay interest on the property tax but only the principal," the independent Belgrade newspaper Nasa Borba quoted Veroljub Stevanovic as saying.

Citizens of Kragujevac were served their property tax returns for 1996 and were due to pay interests rates standing at 200 or more dinars ($35), a large sum in a country where the average monthly wage stands at some $150.
He said the republican authorities owed Kragujevac citizens more than 24 million dinars ($4 million) alone in social security compensations, including child allowance since last March.
"If the republic calculated the interest on its debts we would have nothing against it doing the same for tax returns.
"As it is, I ask that interest on property tax not be paid. I stand behind this position and so does the entire city government," Stevanovic said.
Western diplomats believe that the republican authorities will use every trick in the book to discredit the opposition.
Stevanovic's opposition authorities took charge of the city last month with limited powers and empty coffers to finance the city's decaying infrastructure.

"What we are in charge of is the waterworks, sewerage and garbage disposal. Our biggest problem is the economy which is under complete control of republican bodies," Zoran Zivkovic, the Zajedno Mayor of the neighbouring town of Nis told Reuters.
Zajedno does not even have power over the local police who report to Milosevic's interior ministry in Belgrade.

The electricity network is also under control of the Serbian government. Many state-managed companies in opposition towns have had their headquarters transferred to places safely under the SPS thumb. In effect, Serbian cities must depend on infusions of money from the republic government.

But Zajedno authorities in Kragujevac, unlike in other towns, have won the coveted prize -- control of the local media, a powerful tool ahead of republican presidential and parliamentary elections this year.

Head of the local electronic media Vidosav Stevanovic has promised to tell his audience the "truth about the sorry state of affairs" in their city and elsewhere in the republic, which the voters were so far deprived of over the state media.
In an attempt to reassert authority, Parliament speaker Dragan Tomic said it was time for "fearsome" and "horrible" protests to stop now that Zajedno election victories are being restored.
Students massing for the 86th day of protests were the first to ignore the warning and pressed for the Belgrade University rector to be sacked.
Zoran Djindjic, a Zajedno co-leader, was dismissive of the parliament speaker's comments, saying: "Tomic is afraid of his own people.

"Every spontaneous gathering of people defending their rights appears to him as a threat...This shows how estranged from the people the authorities are and why these protests must take place at all," Djindjic told reporters.
